concerns.concern_text: The cost estimate artifact is explicitly marked TBD with no figures provided. A project of this scale (up to 200M records processed nightly on an autoscaling cluster) cannot proceed through the architecture review gate without a completed cost estimate. This is a gate entry requirement.

The design doc explicitly notes that autoscaling has no maximum node cap. With a 5x swing in record volume (40M to 200M records), unbounded autoscaling represents unbounded cost exposure. A maximum cap must be defined and justified before approval.

The acceptance criterion '100% record coverage' is not testable as stated. It does not define what constitutes a 'covered' record, how coverage is measured, what happens to late-arriving records, nor what the tolerance or escalation path is if the threshold is missed. It needs an operational definition.

The acceptance criterion 'Reconciliation completes by 6am ET' lacks a defined SLO breach procedure, measurement method (e.g., job end timestamp in monitoring), and does not account for the high-end 200M record volume scenario. It is unclear whether the 6am target is achievable at max load.

Beyond the two acceptance criteria, there is no post-launch success metric defined (e.g., exception rate, reconciliation error rate trend, mean time to detect discrepancies). Without these, it will be impossible to evaluate whether v2 is an improvement over v1.

The design references a nightly job processing up to 200M records but provides no egress or data-transfer cost model. If records span regions or involve cross-region data movement, this gap compounded with the missing cost estimate creates material financial risk.

agent_responses.reasoning: This project cannot be approved at the architecture_review_gate for three primary reasons. First, the cost estimate is entirely absent (TBD) — this is a hard gate requirement for any project running autoscaling compute at this record volume. Second, autoscaling has no maximum node cap despite a 5x variance in daily record volume (40M–200M), meaning worst-case compute cost is undefined and unbounded. Third, the acceptance criteria require sharpening: '100% record coverage' has no operational definition, and the 6am ET deadline has no measurement methodology or breach procedure, nor evidence it holds at peak load. Additionally, the project lacks post-launch success metrics to evaluate whether v2 actually improves on v1, and there is no egress cost model for what is a very high-volume data pipeline. All blocking concerns must be resolved before re-submission.

With a record volume that swings between 40M and 200M records, an uncapped autoscaler can produce wildly unpredictable cost spikes and resource contention. A hard ceiling on node count must be defined before proceeding.

The design references cross-service data flows for settlement record ingestion but provides no model for egress costs. Given the 40M–200M record range and potentially cross-region data movement typical of financial reconciliation pipelines, the absence of an egress cost model is a material risk.

concerns.concern_text: The design document contains no documented rollback procedure. For a nightly financial settlement job, a failed or corrupted run must have a clear, tested rollback or reprocessing path to avoid incorrect settlement records impacting downstream systems.

There is no mention of idempotency guarantees for the reconciliation write path. If the nightly job is retried after a partial failure, duplicate writes could corrupt settlement records. Idempotency keys or upsert semantics must be specified.

No circuit breaker or fallback pattern is described for the critical-path upstream data sources the reconciliation job depends on. If a source system degrades at 3am ET, the job could hang indefinitely and miss the 6am ET SLA.
references: design_doc_v3: no circuit breaker or timeout patterns mentioned

concerns.concern_text: No timeout is configured for synchronous calls made by the reconciliation job. Combined with the lack of a circuit breaker, a stalled upstream dependency call could cause the entire job to exceed the 6am ET deadline.

The acceptance criterion '100% record coverage' is not accompanied by a testable definition: how is coverage measured, what constitutes a record, and what is the tolerance window for late-arriving records? Without a precise numeric/testable definition this criterion cannot be validated at release.

agent_responses.reasoning: Both artifacts confirm the project is not ready to pass the architecture review gate. The two most critical blockers are (1) an uncapped autoscaler on a job with a 5x daily volume variance — a production risk that can generate unbounded cloud spend — and (2) a cost estimate that is entirely TBD, which violates basic gate entry criteria for a project of this financial sensitivity. Beyond those blockers, the design is operationally immature: there is no rollback plan, no idempotency guarantee on the write path, no timeout or circuit breaker for upstream dependencies, and no egress cost model. The acceptance criterion '100% record coverage' also lacks a testable, numeric definition. All blocking and high-severity items must be resolved and the design document re-submitted before this gate can be re-evaluated.

concerns.concern_text: The system processes daily settlement records, which almost certainly involves payment card data. There is no mention of a PCI-DSS scope assessment, scoping diagram, or cardholder data environment (CDE) boundary definition anywhere in the design document. This is a blocking concern before any architecture can be approved.

The design document describes an autoscaling cluster processing up to 200M settlement records but makes no mention of encryption at rest for the data store(s) holding those records. Settlement data is highly sensitive financial data and must be encrypted at rest with documented key management.

The design document describes no audit logging mechanism for the reconciliation job. Security-sensitive actions such as record reads, reconciliation overrides, discrepancy resolutions, and administrative access to settlement data must be audit-logged for regulatory and forensic purposes.

Settlement reconciliation records may contain account numbers, names, or other PII/financial identifiers. The design document has no mention of log redaction, masking, or scrubbing controls. Without explicit controls, PII leakage into logs is a likely outcome at this data volume.

No log retention policy is defined anywhere in the design. For financial/settlement data, regulatory frameworks (PCI-DSS, SOX) typically mandate minimum retention periods. Missing this at architecture stage creates compliance risk.

The design does not define IAM roles or permission boundaries for the autoscaling cluster or any service accounts accessing settlement data. Without least-privilege IAM scoping documented at this stage, there is high risk of overly permissive roles being applied by default.

The autoscaling cluster explicitly has no maximum node cap, and volume ranges from 40M to 200M records (5x swing). Without a cost ceiling or max-node constraint, a runaway job or unexpected volume spike can produce unbounded infrastructure spend. This is both a financial and a security (denial-of-wallet) risk.

The cost estimate artifact is explicitly marked TBD with no figures provided. This is a required artifact at the architecture_review_gate and the project cannot be approved without it, especially given the uncapped autoscaling configuration.

agent_responses.reasoning: This architecture review for Daily Settlement Reconciliation v2 surfaces multiple blocking and high-severity security and privacy concerns that prevent approval. Most critically: (1) the system processes settlement records that are highly likely to be in PCI scope, yet no PCI-DSS scope assessment or CDE boundary is documented; (2) there is no encryption-at-rest specification for the data stores; (3) audit logging for security-sensitive reconciliation actions is entirely absent; (4) the design is silent on PII/log redaction controls despite processing up to 200M records containing financial identifiers; (5) no IAM least-privilege model is defined; (6) no log retention policy is documented; (7) the autoscaling cluster has no maximum node cap, creating unbounded exposure; and (8) the cost estimate remains TBD, which is a gate requirement. The project is BLOCKED pending resolution of at minimum the two blocking items (PCI scope review and cost estimate) and the high-severity security controls (encryption at rest, audit logging, PII redaction, IAM scoping).

agent_responses.reasoning: This project cannot pass the architecture review gate in its current state. Two blocking defects are present: (1) the cost estimate is entirely absent (TBD) despite the project involving an uncapped autoscaling cluster with up to 5x daily volume swings—there is no basis for financial approval; and (2) the autoscaler has no maximum node cap, creating unbounded cost exposure. Beyond the blocking items, there are significant high-severity compliance gaps: no PCI scope assessment for a payment settlement system, no egress cost model for a high-volume data job, and no audit logging for a financially regulated workflow. Additionally, vendor SLAs feeding the job are undocumented and no rollback plan exists. The project must resolve at minimum the two blocking defects before resubmission, and the high-severity items should be addressed concurrently given the financial and regulatory nature of the system.
